According to RFC 6265 (the HTTP State Management Mechanism), the cookie-octet definition is:
```

- %x23-2B = # $ % & ' ( ) * + , - . /
- %x2D-3A = - . / 0-9 : 
- %x3C-5B = < = > ? @ A-Z [ 
- %x5D-7E = ] ^ _ ` a-z { | } ~

So according to RFC 6265, colon (`:` - %x3A) is allowed in cookie values.

1. In the old code, `_legal_cookie_chars` included `:` and `_` characters in the set.
2. In the new code, `_token_re = re.compile(r"[\w!#$%&'*+\-.^`|~]*", re.A)` doesn't include `:` (colon) or `_` (underscore) since `\w` in Python regex matches `[a-zA-Z0-9_]` but NOT `:`.

The issue is that cookie values containing `:` are now being quoted (wrapped in double quotes) when they shouldn't be.

According to RFC 6265 (the HTTP State Management Mechanism), the cookie-octet definition is:
```
cookie-octet = %x21 / %x23-2B / %x2D-3A / %x3C-5B / %x5D-7E
```

This means:
- %x21 = !
- %x23-2B = # $ % & ' ( ) * + , - . /
- %x2D-3A = - . / 0-9 : 
- %x3C-5B = < = > ? @ A-Z [ 
- %x5D-7E = ] ^ _ ` a-z { | } ~

So according to RFC 6265, colon (`:` - %x3A) is allowed in cookie values.

Now let's see what characters the current regex includes:
`[\w!#$%&'*+\-.^`|~]`

- `\w` = [a-zA-Z0-9_] - includes underscore
- The rest: !$%&'*+-.^`|~ 

What's missing is `:` (colon). Looking at the issue description, it says:
- The old code included both `:` and `_`
- The new code uses `\w` which includes `_` but NOT `:`


- The fix is to add `:` back to the regex to restore the old behavior and comply with RFC 6265

1. In the old code, `_legal_cookie_chars` included `:` and `_` characters in the set.
2. In the new code, `_token_re = re.compile(r"[\w!#$%&'*+\-.^`|~]*", re.A)` doesn't include `:` (colon) or `_` (underscore) since `\w` in Python regex matches `[a-zA-Z0-9_]` but NOT `:`.

The issue is that cookie values containing `:` are now being quoted (wrapped in double quotes) when they shouldn't be.

According to RFC 6265 (the HTTP State Management Mechanism), the cookie-octet definition is:
```
cookie-octet = %x21 / %x23-2B / %x2D-3A / %x3C-5B / %x5D-7E
```

This means:
- %x21 = !
- %x23-2B = # $ % & ' ( ) * + , - . /
- %x2D-3A = - . / 0-9 : 
- %x3C-5B = < = > ? @ A-Z [ 
- %x5D-7E = ] ^ _ ` a-z { | } ~

So according to RFC 6265, colon (`:` - %x3A) is allowed in cookie values.

Now let's see what characters the current regex includes:
`[\w!#$%&'*+\-.^`|~]`

- `\w` = [a-zA-Z0-9_] - includes underscore
- The rest: !$%&'*+-.^`|~ 

What's missing is `:` (colon). Looking at the issue description, it says:
- The old code included both `:` and `_`
- The new code uses `\w` which includes `_` but NOT `:`


- The fix is to add `:` back to the regex to restore the old behavior and comply with RFC 6265

1. In the old code, `_legal_cookie_chars` included `:` and `_` characters in the set.
2. In the new code, `_token_re = re.compile(r"[\w!#$%&'*+\-.^`|~]*", re.A)` doesn't include `:` (colon) or `_` (underscore) since `\w` in Python regex matches `[a-zA-Z0-9_]` but NOT `:`.

The issue is that cookie values containing `:` are now being quoted (wrapped in double quotes) when they shouldn't be.

According to RFC 6265 (the HTTP State Management Mechanism), the cookie-octet definition is:
```
cookie-octet = %x21 / %x23-2B / %x2D-3A / %x3C-5B / %x5D-7E
```

This means:
- %x21 = !
- %x23-2B = # $ % & ' ( ) * + , - . /
- %x2D-3A = - . / 0-9 : 
- %x3C-5B = < = > ? @ A-Z [ 
- %x5D-7E = ] ^ _ ` a-z { | } ~

So according to RFC 6265, colon (`:` - %x3A) is allowed in cookie values.

Now let's see what characters the current regex includes:
`[\w!#$%&'*+\-.^`|~]`

- `\w` = [a-zA-Z0-9_] - includes underscore
- The rest: !$%&'*+-.^`|~ 

What's missing is `:` (colon). Looking at the issue description, it says:
- The old code included both `:` and `_`
- The new code uses `\w` which includes `_` but NOT `:`


- The fix is to add `:` back to the regex to restore the old behavior and comply with RFC 6265

1. In the old code, `_legal_cookie_chars` included `:` and `_` characters in the set.
2. In the new code, `_token_re = re.compile(r"[\w!#$%&'*+\-.^`|~]*", re.A)` doesn't include `:` (colon) or `_` (underscore) since `\w` in Python regex matches `[a-zA-Z0-9_]` but NOT `:`.

The issue is that cookie values containing `:` are now being quoted (wrapped in double quotes) when they shouldn't be.

According to RFC 6265 (the HTTP State Management Mechanism), the cookie-octet definition is:
```
cookie-octet = %x21 / %x23-2B / %x2D-3A / %x3C-5B / %x5D-7E
```

This means:
- %x21 = !
- %x23-2B = # $ % & ' ( ) * + , - . /
- %x2D-3A = - . / 0-9 : 
- %x3C-5B = < = > ? @ A-Z [ 
- %x5D-7E = ] ^ _ ` a-z { | } ~

So according to RFC 6265, colon (`:` - %x3A) is allowed in cookie values.

Now let's see what characters the current regex includes:
`[\w!#$%&'*+\-.^`|~]`

- `\w` = [a-zA-Z0-9_] - includes underscore
- The rest: !$%&'*+-.^`|~ 

What's missing is `:` (colon). Looking at the issue description, it says:
- The old code included both `:` and `_`
- The new code uses `\w` which includes `_` but NOT `:`


- The fix is to add `:` back to the regex to restore the old behavior and comply with RFC 6265

I have two instances were this behavior can be observed.

1. https://github.com/conda-forge/staged-recipes/pull/29892 . This PR adds 5 patches. The build fails on linux because the patches are not applied.
2. https://github.com/conda-forge/libmodplug-feedstock . In this feedstock a patch is applied to expose symbols for a dynamic library. This doesnt break compilation but does silently ignore the change in modification.

The second case is especially bad. It means that patches that modify logic and don't fix compiler errors are silently ignored! 

Rattler-build 0.40.0 and 0.41.0 dont have this problem. Case number 2 can be build using both older and newer versions. Running `readelf -Ws --dyn-syms <path to libmodplug.so>` should show 600+ symbols but when the package is build with 0.42.0 it only shows 40.

Cleaner api contracts
# Clarification and motivation

Now otter uses an api very similar to other go cache libraries, but unfortunately it is not particularly beautiful and extensible.

For example, now we have `Set(key, value)` and `SetWithTTL(key, value, ttl)` functions, but if we want to add `SetIfAbsent(key, value)` function, we also need `SetIfAbsentWithTTL(key, value, ttl)` function, which doesn't look nice anymore. Especially since when we create the cache in the builder we already know its further behavior and whether it will need ttl or not.

We would like to create a cache with a clean api and with the functions it needs using parameters in the builder. This will allow to provide such api as `Set(key, value, ttl)` and `SetIfAbsent(key, value, ttl)`. Also, since in most cases ttl is the same for all entries in the cache, we don't need to pass it every time at all, further simplifying the api. This will also allow us to use optimizations for the expiration policy, since with the same ttl we only need to maintain a simple fifo queue of items and check their expiration one by one.

# Acceptance criteria

1. A more advanced version of the builder has been implemented
2. Otter provides simpler api contracts
3. Implementation tests are written

   208	func (c *Cache[K, V]) process() {
   209		bufferCapacity := 64
   210		buffer := make([]node.WriteTask[K, V], 0, bufferCapacity)
   211		deleted := make([]*node.Node[K, V], 0, bufferCapacity)
   212		i := 0
   213		for {
   214			task := c.writeBuffer.Remove()
   215	
   216			if task.IsClear() || task.IsClose() {
   217				buffer = clearBuffer(buffer)
   218				c.writeBuffer.Clear()
   219	
   220				c.evictionMutex.Lock()
   221				c.policy.Clear()
   222				c.expirePolicy.Clear()
   223				if task.IsClose() {
   224					c.isClosed = true
   225				}
   226				c.evictionMutex.Unlock()
   227	
   228				c.doneClear <- struct{}{}
   229				if task.IsClose() {
   230					break
   231				}
   232				continue
   233			}
   234	
   235			buffer = append(buffer, task)
   236			i++
   237			if i >= bufferCapacity {
   238				i -= bufferCapacity
   239	
   240				c.evictionMutex.Lock()
   241	
   242				for _, t := range buffer {
   243					switch {
   244					case t.IsDelete():
   245						c.expirePolicy.Delete(t.Node())
   246					case t.IsAdd():
   247						c.expirePolicy.Add(t.Node())
   248					case t.IsUpdate():
   249						c.expirePolicy.Delete(t.OldNode())
   250						c.expirePolicy.Add(t.Node())
   251					}
   252				}
   253	
   254				d := c.policy.Write(deleted, buffer)
   255				for _, n := range d {
   256					c.expirePolicy.Delete(n)
   257				}
   258	
   259				c.evictionMutex.Unlock()
   260	
   261				for _, n := range d {
   262					c.hashmap.EvictNode(n)
   263				}
   264	
   265				buffer = clearBuffer(buffer)
   266				deleted = clearBuffer(deleted)
   267			}
   268		}
   269	}

// CollectStats enables statistics collection for the cache.
func (b *Builder[K, V]) CollectStats() *Builder[K, V] {
	b.statsEnabled = true
	return b

func (b *Builder[K, V]) WithTTL(ttl time.Duration) (*ConstTTLBuilder[K, V], error) {
	if ttl <= 0 {
		return nil, ErrIllegalTTL
	}
	return &ConstTTLBuilder[K, V]{builder: b, ttl: ttl}, nil
}

// WithVariableTTL switches the builder to variable TTL mode.
func (b *Builder[K, V]) WithVariableTTL() *VariableTTLBuilder[K, V] {
	return &VariableTTLBuilder[K, V]{builder: b}
}

// ConstTTLBuilder builds a cache with constant TTL.
type ConstTTLBuilder[K comparable, V any] struct {
	builder *Builder[K, V]
	ttl     time.Duration
}

// CollectStats enables statistics collection.
func (b *ConstTTLBuilder[K, V]) CollectStats() *ConstTTLBuilder[K, V] {
	b.builder.statsEnabled = true
	return b
}

// Cost sets a custom cost function.
func (b *ConstTTLBuilder[K, V]) Cost(costFunc func(key K, value V) uint32) *ConstTTLBuilder[K, V] {
	b.builder.costFunc = costFunc
	return b
}

// Build creates a cache with constant TTL.
func (b *ConstTTLBuilder[K, V]) Build() (*Cache[K, V], error) {
	if b.ttl <= 0 {
		return nil, ErrIllegalTTL
	}
	if err := b.builder.validate(); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	config := b.builder.toConfig()
	config.TTL = b.ttl
	return NewCache(config), nil
}

// VariableTTLBuilder builds a cache with variable TTL.
type VariableTTLBuilder[K comparable, V any] struct {
	builder *Builder[K, V]
}

// CollectStats enables statistics collection.
func (b *VariableTTLBuilder[K, V]) CollectStats() *VariableTTLBuilder[K, V] {
	b.builder.statsEnabled = true
	return b
}

// Cost sets a custom cost function.
func (b *VariableTTLBuilder[K, V]) Cost(costFunc func(key K, value V) uint32) *VariableTTLBuilder[K, V] {
	b.builder.costFunc = costFunc
	return b
}

// Build creates a cache with variable TTL support.
func (b *VariableTTLBuilder[K, V]) Build() (*CacheWithVariableTTL[K, V], error) {
	if err := b.builder.validate(); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	config := b.builder.toConfig()
	return NewCacheWithVariableTTL(config), nil
}

<issue_description>
Cleaner api contracts
# Clarification and motivation

Now otter uses an api very similar to other go cache libraries, but unfortunately it is not particularly beautiful and extensible.

For example, now we have `Set(key, value)` and `SetWithTTL(key, value, ttl)` functions, but if we want to add `SetIfAbsent(key, value)` function, we also need `SetIfAbsentWithTTL(key, value, ttl)` function, which doesn't look nice anymore. Especially since when we create the cache in the builder we already know its further behavior and whether it will need ttl or not.

We would like to create a cache with a clean api and with the functions it needs using parameters in the builder. This will allow to provide such api as `Set(key, value, ttl)` and `SetIfAbsent(key, value, ttl)`. Also, since in most cases ttl is the same for all entries in the cache, we don't need to pass it every time at all, further simplifying the api. This will also allow us to use optimizations for the expiration policy, since with the same ttl we only need to maintain a simple fifo queue of items and check their expiration one by one.

# Acceptance criteria

1. A more advanced version of the builder has been implemented
2. Otter provides simpler api contracts
3. Implementation tests are written

Cleaner api contracts
# Clarification and motivation

Now otter uses an api very similar to other go cache libraries, but unfortunately it is not particularly beautiful and extensible.

For example, now we have `Set(key, value)` and `SetWithTTL(key, value, ttl)` functions, but if we want to add `SetIfAbsent(key, value)` function, we also need `SetIfAbsentWithTTL(key, value, ttl)` function, which doesn't look nice anymore. Especially since when we create the cache in the builder we already know its further behavior and whether it will need ttl or not.

We would like to create a cache with a clean api and with the functions it needs using parameters in the builder. This will allow to provide such api as `Set(key, value, ttl)` and `SetIfAbsent(key, value, ttl)`. Also, since in most cases ttl is the same for all entries in the cache, we don't need to pass it every time at all, further simplifying the api. This will also allow us to use optimizations for the expiration policy, since with the same ttl we only need to maintain a simple fifo queue of items and check their expiration one by one.

# Acceptance criteria

1. A more advanced version of the builder has been implemented
2. Otter provides simpler api contracts
3. Implementation tests are written

    45	// Cache is a structure performs a best-effort bounding of a hash table using eviction algorithm
    46	// to determine which entries to evict when the capacity is exceeded.
    47	type Cache[K comparable, V any] struct {
    48		hashmap       *hashtable.Map[K, V]
    49		policy        *s3fifo.Policy[K, V]
    50		expirePolicy  *expire.Policy[K, V]
    51		stats         *stats.Stats
    52		readBuffers   []*lossy.Buffer[node.Node[K, V]]
    53		writeBuffer   *queue.MPSC[node.WriteTask[K, V]]
    54		evictionMutex sync.Mutex
    55		closeOnce     sync.Once
    56		isClosed      bool
    57		doneClear     chan struct{}
    58		costFunc      func(key K, value V) uint32
    59		capacity      int
    60		mask          uint32
    61	}

    63	// NewCache returns a new cache instance based on the settings from Config.
    64	//
    65	// You should always prefer to create a cache using Builder instead of this method.
    66	func NewCache[K comparable, V any](c Config[K, V]) *Cache[K, V] {
    67		parallelism := xruntime.Parallelism()
    68		roundedParallelism := int(xmath.RoundUpPowerOf2(parallelism))
    69		writeBufferCapacity := 128 * roundedParallelism
    70		readBuffersCount := 4 * roundedParallelism
    71	
    72		readBuffers := make([]*lossy.Buffer[node.Node[K, V]], 0, readBuffersCount)
    73		for i := 0; i < readBuffersCount; i++ {
    74			readBuffers = append(readBuffers, lossy.New[node.Node[K, V]]())
    75		}
    76	
    77		cache := &Cache[K, V]{
    78			hashmap:     hashtable.New[K, V](),
    79			policy:      s3fifo.NewPolicy[K, V](uint32(c.Capacity)),
    80			readBuffers: readBuffers,
    81			writeBuffer: queue.NewMPSC[node.WriteTask[K, V]](writeBufferCapacity),
    82			doneClear:   make(chan struct{}),
    83			mask:        uint32(readBuffersCount - 1),
    84			costFunc:    c.CostFunc,
    85			capacity:    c.Capacity,
    86		}
    87	
    88		cache.expirePolicy = expire.NewPolicy[K, V]()
    89		if c.StatsEnabled {
    90			cache.stats = stats.New()
    91		}
    92	
    93		unixtime.Start()
    94		go cache.process()
    95		go cache.cleanup()
    96	
    97		return cache
    98	}

   104	// Has checks if there is an item with the given key in the cache.
   105	func (c *Cache[K, V]) Has(key K) bool {
   106		_, ok := c.Get(key)
   107		return ok

   110	// Get returns the value associated with the key in this cache.
   111	func (c *Cache[K, V]) Get(key K) (V, bool) {
   112		got, ok := c.hashmap.Get(key)
   113		if !ok {
   114			c.stats.IncMisses()
   115			return zeroValue[V](), false
   116		}
   117	
   118		if got.IsExpired() {
   119			c.writeBuffer.Insert(node.NewDeleteTask(got))
   120			c.stats.IncMisses()
   121			return zeroValue[V](), false
   122		}
   123	
   124		c.afterGet(got)
   125		c.stats.IncHits()
   126	
   127		return got.Value(), ok
   128	}

   130	func (c *Cache[K, V]) afterGet(got *node.Node[K, V]) {
   131		idx := c.getReadBufferIdx()
   132		pb := c.readBuffers[idx].Add(got)
   133		if pb != nil {
   134			c.evictionMutex.Lock()
   135			c.policy.Read(pb.Returned)
   136			c.evictionMutex.Unlock()
   137	
   138			c.readBuffers[idx].Free()
   139		}
   140	}

   142	// Set associates the value with the key in this cache.
   143	//
   144	// If it returns false, then the key-value item had too much cost and the Set was dropped.

   149	// SetWithTTL associates the value with the key in this cache and sets the custom ttl for this key-value item.
   150	//
   151	// If it returns false, then the key-value item had too much cost and the SetWithTTL was dropped.
   152	func (c *Cache[K, V]) SetWithTTL(key K, value V, ttl time.Duration) bool {

   154		expiration := unixtime.Now() + uint32(ttl)
   155		return c.set(key, value, expiration)
   156	}

   158	func (c *Cache[K, V]) set(key K, value V, expiration uint32) bool {
   159		cost := c.costFunc(key, value)
   160		if cost > c.policy.MaxAvailableCost() {
   161			return false
   162		}
   163	
   164		n := node.New(key, value, expiration, cost)
   165		evicted := c.hashmap.Set(n)
   166		if evicted != nil {
   167			// update
   168			c.writeBuffer.Insert(node.NewUpdateTask(n, evicted))
   169		} else {
   170			// insert
   171			c.writeBuffer.Insert(node.NewAddTask(n))
   172		}
   173	
   174		return true
   175	}

   177	// Delete removes the association for this key from the cache.
   178	func (c *Cache[K, V]) Delete(key K) {
   179		deleted := c.hashmap.Delete(key)
   180		if deleted != nil {
   181			c.writeBuffer.Insert(node.NewDeleteTask(deleted))
   182		}
   183	}

   185	func (c *Cache[K, V]) cleanup() {
   186		expired := make([]*node.Node[K, V], 0, 128)
   187		for {
   188			time.Sleep(time.Second)
   189	
   190			c.evictionMutex.Lock()
   191			if c.isClosed {
   192				return
   193			}
   194	
   195			e := c.expirePolicy.RemoveExpired(expired)
   196			c.policy.Delete(e)
   197	
   198			c.evictionMutex.Unlock()
   199	
   200			for _, n := range e {
   201				c.hashmap.EvictNode(n)
   202			}
   203	
   204			expired = clearBuffer(expired)
   205		}
   206	}

   208	func (c *Cache[K, V]) process() {
   209		bufferCapacity := 64
   210		buffer := make([]node.WriteTask[K, V], 0, bufferCapacity)
   211		deleted := make([]*node.Node[K, V], 0, bufferCapacity)
   212		i := 0
   213		for {
   214			task := c.writeBuffer.Remove()
   215	
   216			if task.IsClear() || task.IsClose() {
   217				buffer = clearBuffer(buffer)
   218				c.writeBuffer.Clear()
   219	
   220				c.evictionMutex.Lock()
   221				c.policy.Clear()
   222				c.expirePolicy.Clear()
   223				if task.IsClose() {
   224					c.isClosed = true
   225				}
   226				c.evictionMutex.Unlock()
   227	
   228				c.doneClear <- struct{}{}
   229				if task.IsClose() {
   230					break
   231				}
   232				continue
   233			}
   234	
   235			buffer = append(buffer, task)
   236			i++
   237			if i >= bufferCapacity {
   238				i -= bufferCapacity
   239	
   240				c.evictionMutex.Lock()
   241	
   242				for _, t := range buffer {
   243					switch {
   244					case t.IsDelete():
   245						c.expirePolicy.Delete(t.Node())
   246					case t.IsAdd():
   247						c.expirePolicy.Add(t.Node())
   248					case t.IsUpdate():
   249						c.expirePolicy.Delete(t.OldNode())
   250						c.expirePolicy.Add(t.Node())
   251					}
   252				}
   253	
   254				d := c.policy.Write(deleted, buffer)
   255				for _, n := range d {
   256					c.expirePolicy.Delete(n)
   257				}
   258	
   259				c.evictionMutex.Unlock()
   260	
   261				for _, n := range d {
   262					c.hashmap.EvictNode(n)
   263				}
   264	
   265				buffer = clearBuffer(buffer)
   266				deleted = clearBuffer(deleted)
   267			}
   268		}
   269	}

Cleaner api contracts
# Clarification and motivation

Now otter uses an api very similar to other go cache libraries, but unfortunately it is not particularly beautiful and extensible.

For example, now we have `Set(key, value)` and `SetWithTTL(key, value, ttl)` functions, but if we want to add `SetIfAbsent(key, value)` function, we also need `SetIfAbsentWithTTL(key, value, ttl)` function, which doesn't look nice anymore. Especially since when we create the cache in the builder we already know its further behavior and whether it will need ttl or not.

We would like to create a cache with a clean api and with the functions it needs using parameters in the builder. This will allow to provide such api as `Set(key, value, ttl)` and `SetIfAbsent(key, value, ttl)`. Also, since in most cases ttl is the same for all entries in the cache, we don't need to pass it every time at all, further simplifying the api. This will also allow us to use optimizations for the expiration policy, since with the same ttl we only need to maintain a simple fifo queue of items and check their expiration one by one.

# Acceptance criteria

1. A more advanced version of the builder has been implemented
2. Otter provides simpler api contracts
3. Implementation tests are written

Cleaner api contracts
# Clarification and motivation

Now otter uses an api very similar to other go cache libraries, but unfortunately it is not particularly beautiful and extensible.

For example, now we have `Set(key, value)` and `SetWithTTL(key, value, ttl)` functions, but if we want to add `SetIfAbsent(key, value)` function, we also need `SetIfAbsentWithTTL(key, value, ttl)` function, which doesn't look nice anymore. Especially since when we create the cache in the builder we already know its further behavior and whether it will need ttl or not.

We would like to create a cache with a clean api and with the functions it needs using parameters in the builder. This will allow to provide such api as `Set(key, value, ttl)` and `SetIfAbsent(key, value, ttl)`. Also, since in most cases ttl is the same for all entries in the cache, we don't need to pass it every time at all, further simplifying the api. This will also allow us to use optimizations for the expiration policy, since with the same ttl we only need to maintain a simple fifo queue of items and check their expiration one by one.

   276	func newOptimal(capacity uint64) *optimal {
   277		return &optimal{
   278			capacity: capacity,
   279			hits:     make(map[uint64]uint64),
   280			access:   make([]uint64, 0),
   281		}
   282	}
   283	
   284	func (o *optimal) Get(key uint64) {
   285		o.hits[key]++
   286		o.access = append(o.access, key)
   287	}

   289	func (o *optimal) Ratio() float64 {
   290		look := make(map[uint64]struct{}, o.capacity)
   291		data := &optimalHeap{}
   292		heap.Init(data)
   293		hits := 0
   294		misses := 0
   295		for _, key := range o.access {
   296			if _, has := look[key]; has {
   297				hits++
   298				continue
   299			}
   300			if uint64(data.Len()) >= o.capacity {
   301				victim := heap.Pop(data)
   302				delete(look, victim.(*optimalItem).key)
   303			}
   304			misses++
   305			look[key] = struct{}{}
   306			heap.Push(data, &optimalItem{key, o.hits[key]})
   307		}
   308		if hits == 0 && misses == 0 {
   309			return 0.0
   310		}
   311		return float64(hits) / float64(hits+misses)
   312	}

   317	}

   322	func (h optimalHeap) Less(i, j int) bool { return h[i].hits < h[j].hits }
   323	func (h optimalHeap) Swap(i, j int)      { h[i], h[j] = h[j], h[i] }

   325	func (h *optimalHeap) Push(x any) {

Consider the following PR description:
DateTime field fails to handle oversized timestamps

Description
	 
		(last modified by User)
	 
When using the DateTime field with timestamp or timestamp_ms formats, the library fails to properly handle oversized timestamp values. This causes unexpected errors when deserializing very large timestamp values.

For example, when trying to deserialize an extremely large timestamp value like 99999999999999999, instead of getting a proper ValidationError with a message indicating that the timestamp is invalid, the application crashes with either an OSError or OverflowError depending on the system.

Here's a simple reproduction script:

```python
from marshmallow import Schema, fields

class MySchema(Schema):
    created_at = fields.DateTime(format="timestamp")

schema = MySchema()
try:
    result = schema.load({"created_at": 99999999999999999})
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error type: {type(e).__name__}")
    print(f"Error message: {str(e)}")
```

The expected behavior would be for the library to catch these errors and convert them to proper ValidationErrors, as it did in previous versions. This is important for applications that need to handle potentially malicious or malformed input data gracefully.

I encountered this issue in a production environment where our API was crashing when receiving certain timestamp values from external sources, rather than returning a proper validation error response.

<issue_description>
client/rs: error when issuer discovery has no introspection endpoint
**Describe the bug**
When an issuer does not provide an introspection endpoint during discovery, `newResourceServer()` fails with:
```
introspectURL and/or tokenURL is empty: please provide with either `WithStaticEndpoints` or a discovery url
```
Note that a token endpoint is always provided by the issuer.

According to the OpenID specs for [Discovery responses](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-discovery-1_0.html#ProviderConfigurationResponse), an introspection endpoint is not mandatory (not defined in the response object) while the token endpoint is required.

Three examples of issuers that do not provide any introspection endpoint are:
* Google: <https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>
* Spotify: <https://accounts.spotify.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>
* PayPal: <https://www.paypal.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>

This is because of the following (incorrect) check after discovery that assumes that both endpoints must be present:
https://github.com/zitadel/oidc/blob/9e624986aaf6eb8854ffc4702d7d1cc755919ff5/pkg/client/rs/resource_server.go#L83-L85

In reality, the introspection endpoint is valid to be empty.

**To Reproduce**
Consider the following demonstration Go program:
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	"github.com/zitadel/oidc/v2/pkg/client/rs"
)

const (
	Issuer = "https://accounts.google.com"
//	Issuer = "https://accounts.spotify.com"
//	Issuer = "https://www.paypal.com"
	ClientId = "client-id"
	ClientSecret = "client-secret"
)

func main() {
	rscc, err := rs.NewResourceServerClientCredentials(
		Issuer,
		ClientId,
		ClientSecret,
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", rscc)

	res, err := rs.Introspect(nil, rscc, "test-token")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", res)
}
```
When running the above program, an panic is emitted after the error from `NewResourceServerClientCredentials()`:
```
$ go run main.go
panic: introspectURL and/or tokenURL is empty: please provide with either `WithStaticEndpoints` or a discovery url

exit status 2
```

**Expected behavior**
Given that in the demonstration program above I'm using the discovery mechanism, I expect it to not fail when the issuer does not provide an introspection endpoint during discovery as it is an optional feature.

Instead, I expect the `rscc` object to be correctly instantiated and a future call to `rs.Introspect()` fails with an error related to the introspection endpoint not being set. This would allow to still use `rscc` (for the authorizer functionality) but without introspection support.

It can be argued that if an issuer is known to not provide an introspection endpoint, it can be given statically using `WithStaticEndpoints("", "https://some.host/introspection-endpoint")` (or a dummy value) but is highly unlikely that a provider has a manual introspection endpoint and does not provide it in discovery. This would just propagate a confusing error later during `rs.Introspect()`.

**Potential Solution**
I propose to instead accept that discovery may not provide an introspection endpoint, do not fail in this situation, and add a check for an empty introspection endpoint in `rs.Introspect()` to clearly indicate that the issuer does not support introspection.

In addition, discovery should only set `introspectURL` or `tokenURL` if they were not given in static endpoint arguments.

If the above makes sense, I already have this logic implemented here:
https://github.com/hhromic/oidc/compare/main...hhromic:oidc:fix-rs-discovery

As it can be seen, I also made a set of unit tests that cover this issue.
Let me know if you agree with the above proposal to open a PR with these changes.

<issue_description>
client/rs: error when issuer discovery has no introspection endpoint
**Describe the bug**
When an issuer does not provide an introspection endpoint during discovery, `newResourceServer()` fails with:
```
introspectURL and/or tokenURL is empty: please provide with either `WithStaticEndpoints` or a discovery url
```
Note that a token endpoint is always provided by the issuer.

According to the OpenID specs for [Discovery responses](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-discovery-1_0.html#ProviderConfigurationResponse), an introspection endpoint is not mandatory (not defined in the response object) while the token endpoint is required.

Three examples of issuers that do not provide any introspection endpoint are:
* Google: <https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>
* Spotify: <https://accounts.spotify.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>
* PayPal: <https://www.paypal.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>

This is because of the following (incorrect) check after discovery that assumes that both endpoints must be present:
https://github.com/zitadel/oidc/blob/9e624986aaf6eb8854ffc4702d7d1cc755919ff5/pkg/client/rs/resource_server.go#L83-L85

In reality, the introspection endpoint is valid to be empty.

**To Reproduce**
Consider the following demonstration Go program:
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	"github.com/zitadel/oidc/v2/pkg/client/rs"
)

const (
	Issuer = "https://accounts.google.com"
//	Issuer = "https://accounts.spotify.com"
//	Issuer = "https://www.paypal.com"
	ClientId = "client-id"
	ClientSecret = "client-secret"
)

func main() {
	rscc, err := rs.NewResourceServerClientCredentials(
		Issuer,
		ClientId,
		ClientSecret,
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", rscc)

	res, err := rs.Introspect(nil, rscc, "test-token")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", res)
}
```
When running the above program, an panic is emitted after the error from `NewResourceServerClientCredentials()`:
```
$ go run main.go
panic: introspectURL and/or tokenURL is empty: please provide with either `WithStaticEndpoints` or a discovery url

exit status 2
```

**Expected behavior**
Given that in the demonstration program above I'm using the discovery mechanism, I expect it to not fail when the issuer does not provide an introspection endpoint during discovery as it is an optional feature.

Instead, I expect the `rscc` object to be correctly instantiated and a future call to `rs.Introspect()` fails with an error related to the introspection endpoint not being set. This would allow to still use `rscc` (for the authorizer functionality) but without introspection support.

It can be argued that if an issuer is known to not provide an introspection endpoint, it can be given statically using `WithStaticEndpoints("", "https://some.host/introspection-endpoint")` (or a dummy value) but is highly unlikely that a provider has a manual introspection endpoint and does not provide it in discovery. This would just propagate a confusing error later during `rs.Introspect()`.

**Potential Solution**
I propose to instead accept that discovery may not provide an introspection endpoint, do not fail in this situation, and add a check for an empty introspection endpoint in `rs.Introspect()` to clearly indicate that the issuer does not support introspection.

In addition, discovery should only set `introspectURL` or `tokenURL` if they were not given in static endpoint arguments.

If the above makes sense, I already have this logic implemented here:
https://github.com/hhromic/oidc/compare/main...hhromic:oidc:fix-rs-discovery

As it can be seen, I also made a set of unit tests that cover this issue.
Let me know if you agree with the above proposal to open a PR with these changes.

<issue_description>
client/rs: error when issuer discovery has no introspection endpoint
**Describe the bug**
When an issuer does not provide an introspection endpoint during discovery, `newResourceServer()` fails with:
```
introspectURL and/or tokenURL is empty: please provide with either `WithStaticEndpoints` or a discovery url
```
Note that a token endpoint is always provided by the issuer.

According to the OpenID specs for [Discovery responses](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-discovery-1_0.html#ProviderConfigurationResponse), an introspection endpoint is not mandatory (not defined in the response object) while the token endpoint is required.

Three examples of issuers that do not provide any introspection endpoint are:
* Google: <https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>
* Spotify: <https://accounts.spotify.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>
* PayPal: <https://www.paypal.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>

This is because of the following (incorrect) check after discovery that assumes that both endpoints must be present:
https://github.com/zitadel/oidc/blob/9e624986aaf6eb8854ffc4702d7d1cc755919ff5/pkg/client/rs/resource_server.go#L83-L85

In reality, the introspection endpoint is valid to be empty.

**To Reproduce**
Consider the following demonstration Go program:
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	"github.com/zitadel/oidc/v2/pkg/client/rs"
)

const (
	Issuer = "https://accounts.google.com"
//	Issuer = "https://accounts.spotify.com"
//	Issuer = "https://www.paypal.com"
	ClientId = "client-id"
	ClientSecret = "client-secret"
)

func main() {
	rscc, err := rs.NewResourceServerClientCredentials(
		Issuer,
		ClientId,
		ClientSecret,
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", rscc)

	res, err := rs.Introspect(nil, rscc, "test-token")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", res)
}
```
When running the above program, an panic is emitted after the error from `NewResourceServerClientCredentials()`:
```
$ go run main.go
panic: introspectURL and/or tokenURL is empty: please provide with either `WithStaticEndpoints` or a discovery url

exit status 2
```

**Expected behavior**
Given that in the demonstration program above I'm using the discovery mechanism, I expect it to not fail when the issuer does not provide an introspection endpoint during discovery as it is an optional feature.

Instead, I expect the `rscc` object to be correctly instantiated and a future call to `rs.Introspect()` fails with an error related to the introspection endpoint not being set. This would allow to still use `rscc` (for the authorizer functionality) but without introspection support.

It can be argued that if an issuer is known to not provide an introspection endpoint, it can be given statically using `WithStaticEndpoints("", "https://some.host/introspection-endpoint")` (or a dummy value) but is highly unlikely that a provider has a manual introspection endpoint and does not provide it in discovery. This would just propagate a confusing error later during `rs.Introspect()`.

**Potential Solution**
I propose to instead accept that discovery may not provide an introspection endpoint, do not fail in this situation, and add a check for an empty introspection endpoint in `rs.Introspect()` to clearly indicate that the issuer does not support introspection.

In addition, discovery should only set `introspectURL` or `tokenURL` if they were not given in static endpoint arguments.

If the above makes sense, I already have this logic implemented here:
https://github.com/hhromic/oidc/compare/main...hhromic:oidc:fix-rs-discovery

As it can be seen, I also made a set of unit tests that cover this issue.
Let me know if you agree with the above proposal to open a PR with these changes.

	TokenEndpoint() string

type resourceServer struct {
	issuer        string
	tokenURL      string
	introspectURL string
	httpClient    *http.Client
	authFn        func() (interface{}, error)
}

func (r *resourceServer) IntrospectionURL() string {
	return r.introspectURL
}

func (r *resourceServer) TokenEndpoint() string {
	return r.tokenURL
}

func (r *resourceServer) HttpClient() *http.Client {
	return r.httpClient
}

func (r *resourceServer) AuthFn() (interface{}, error) {
	return r.authFn()
}

func NewResourceServerClientCredentials(issuer, clientID, clientSecret string, option ...Option) (ResourceServer, error) {
	authorizer := func() (interface{}, error) {
		return httphelper.AuthorizeBasic(clientID, clientSecret), nil
	}
	return newResourceServer(issuer, authorizer, option...)
}

func NewResourceServerJWTProfile(issuer, clientID, keyID string, key []byte, options ...Option) (ResourceServer, error) {
	signer, err := client.NewSignerFromPrivateKeyByte(key, keyID)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	authorizer := func() (interface{}, error) {
		assertion, err := client.SignedJWTProfileAssertion(clientID, []string{issuer}, time.Hour, signer)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		return client.ClientAssertionFormAuthorization(assertion), nil
	}
	return newResourceServer(issuer, authorizer, options...)
}

func newResourceServer(issuer string, authorizer func() (interface{}, error), options ...Option) (*resourceServer, error) {
	rs := &resourceServer{
		issuer:     issuer,
		httpClient: httphelper.DefaultHTTPClient,
	}
	for _, optFunc := range options {
		optFunc(rs)
	}
	if rs.tokenURL == "" {
		config, err := client.Discover(rs.issuer, rs.httpClient)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		rs.tokenURL = config.TokenEndpoint
		rs.introspectURL = config.IntrospectionEndpoint
	}
	if rs.tokenURL == "" {
		return nil, errors.New("tokenURL is empty: please provide with either `WithStaticEndpoints` or a discovery url")
	}
	rs.authFn = authorizer
	return rs, nil
}

func NewResourceServerFromKeyFile(issuer, path string, options ...Option) (ResourceServer, error) {
	c, err := client.ConfigFromKeyFile(path)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	return NewResourceServerJWTProfile(issuer, c.ClientID, c.KeyID, []byte(c.Key), options...)
}

type Option func(*resourceServer)

// WithClient provides the ability to set an http client to be used for the resource server
func WithClient(client *http.Client) Option {
	return func(server *resourceServer) {
		server.httpClient = client
	}
}

// WithStaticEndpoints provides the ability to set static token and introspect URL
func WithStaticEndpoints(tokenURL, introspectURL string) Option {
	return func(server *resourceServer) {
		server.tokenURL = tokenURL
		server.introspectURL = introspectURL
	}
}

func Introspect(ctx context.Context, rp ResourceServer, token string) (*oidc.IntrospectionResponse, error) {
	if rp.IntrospectionURL() == "" {
		return nil, errors.New("introspection URL is empty: please provide with either `WithStaticEndpoints` or a discovery url")
	}
	authFn, err := rp.AuthFn()
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	req, err := httphelper.FormRequest(rp.IntrospectionURL(), &oidc.IntrospectionRequest{Token: token}, client.Encoder, authFn)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	resp := new(oidc.IntrospectionResponse)
	if err := httphelper.HttpRequest(rp.HttpClient(), req, resp); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	return resp, nil
}

<issue_description>
client/rs: error when issuer discovery has no introspection endpoint
**Describe the bug**
When an issuer does not provide an introspection endpoint during discovery, `newResourceServer()` fails with:
```
introspectURL and/or tokenURL is empty: please provide with either `WithStaticEndpoints` or a discovery url
```
Note that a token endpoint is always provided by the issuer.

According to the OpenID specs for [Discovery responses](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-discovery-1_0.html#ProviderConfigurationResponse), an introspection endpoint is not mandatory (not defined in the response object) while the token endpoint is required.

Three examples of issuers that do not provide any introspection endpoint are:
* Google: <https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>
* Spotify: <https://accounts.spotify.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>
* PayPal: <https://www.paypal.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>

This is because of the following (incorrect) check after discovery that assumes that both endpoints must be present:
https://github.com/zitadel/oidc/blob/9e624986aaf6eb8854ffc4702d7d1cc755919ff5/pkg/client/rs/resource_server.go#L83-L85

In reality, the introspection endpoint is valid to be empty.

**To Reproduce**
Consider the following demonstration Go program:
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	"github.com/zitadel/oidc/v2/pkg/client/rs"
)

const (
	Issuer = "https://accounts.google.com"
//	Issuer = "https://accounts.spotify.com"
//	Issuer = "https://www.paypal.com"
	ClientId = "client-id"
	ClientSecret = "client-secret"
)

func main() {
	rscc, err := rs.NewResourceServerClientCredentials(
		Issuer,
		ClientId,
		ClientSecret,
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", rscc)

	res, err := rs.Introspect(nil, rscc, "test-token")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", res)
}
```
When running the above program, an panic is emitted after the error from `NewResourceServerClientCredentials()`:
```
$ go run main.go
panic: introspectURL and/or tokenURL is empty: please provide with either `WithStaticEndpoints` or a discovery url

exit status 2
```

**Expected behavior**
Given that in the demonstration program above I'm using the discovery mechanism, I expect it to not fail when the issuer does not provide an introspection endpoint during discovery as it is an optional feature.

Instead, I expect the `rscc` object to be correctly instantiated and a future call to `rs.Introspect()` fails with an error related to the introspection endpoint not being set. This would allow to still use `rscc` (for the authorizer functionality) but without introspection support.

It can be argued that if an issuer is known to not provide an introspection endpoint, it can be given statically using `WithStaticEndpoints("", "https://some.host/introspection-endpoint")` (or a dummy value) but is highly unlikely that a provider has a manual introspection endpoint and does not provide it in discovery. This would just propagate a confusing error later during `rs.Introspect()`.

**Potential Solution**
I propose to instead accept that discovery may not provide an introspection endpoint, do not fail in this situation, and add a check for an empty introspection endpoint in `rs.Introspect()` to clearly indicate that the issuer does not support introspection.

In addition, discovery should only set `introspectURL` or `tokenURL` if they were not given in static endpoint arguments.

If the above makes sense, I already have this logic implemented here:
https://github.com/hhromic/oidc/compare/main...hhromic:oidc:fix-rs-discovery

As it can be seen, I also made a set of unit tests that cover this issue.
Let me know if you agree with the above proposal to open a PR with these changes.

<issue_description>
client/rs: error when issuer discovery has no introspection endpoint
**Describe the bug**
When an issuer does not provide an introspection endpoint during discovery, `newResourceServer()` fails with:
```
introspectURL and/or tokenURL is empty: please provide with either `WithStaticEndpoints` or a discovery url
```
Note that a token endpoint is always provided by the issuer.

According to the OpenID specs for [Discovery responses](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-discovery-1_0.html#ProviderConfigurationResponse), an introspection endpoint is not mandatory (not defined in the response object) while the token endpoint is required.

Three examples of issuers that do not provide any introspection endpoint are:
* Google: <https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>
* Spotify: <https://accounts.spotify.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>
* PayPal: <https://www.paypal.com/.well-known/openid-configuration>

This is because of the following (incorrect) check after discovery that assumes that both endpoints must be present:
https://github.com/zitadel/oidc/blob/9e624986aaf6eb8854ffc4702d7d1cc755919ff5/pkg/client/rs/resource_server.go#L83-L85

In reality, the introspection endpoint is valid to be empty.

**To Reproduce**
Consider the following demonstration Go program:
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	"github.com/zitadel/oidc/v2/pkg/client/rs"
)

const (
	Issuer = "https://accounts.google.com"
//	Issuer = "https://accounts.spotify.com"
//	Issuer = "https://www.paypal.com"
	ClientId = "client-id"
	ClientSecret = "client-secret"
)

func main() {
	rscc, err := rs.NewResourceServerClientCredentials(
		Issuer,
		ClientId,
		ClientSecret,
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", rscc)

	res, err := rs.Introspect(nil, rscc, "test-token")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", res)
}
```
When running the above program, an panic is emitted after the error from `NewResourceServerClientCredentials()`:
```
$ go run main.go
panic: introspectURL and/or tokenURL is empty: please provide with either `WithStaticEndpoints` or a discovery url

exit status 2
```

**Expected behavior**
Given that in the demonstration program above I'm using the discovery mechanism, I expect it to not fail when the issuer does not provide an introspection endpoint during discovery as it is an optional feature.

Instead, I expect the `rscc` object to be correctly instantiated and a future call to `rs.Introspect()` fails with an error related to the introspection endpoint not being set. This would allow to still use `rscc` (for the authorizer functionality) but without introspection support.

It can be argued that if an issuer is known to not provide an introspection endpoint, it can be given statically using `WithStaticEndpoints("", "https://some.host/introspection-endpoint")` (or a dummy value) but is highly unlikely that a provider has a manual introspection endpoint and does not provide it in discovery. This would just propagate a confusing error later during `rs.Introspect()`.

**Potential Solution**
I propose to instead accept that discovery may not provide an introspection endpoint, do not fail in this situation, and add a check for an empty introspection endpoint in `rs.Introspect()` to clearly indicate that the issuer does not support introspection.

In addition, discovery should only set `introspectURL` or `tokenURL` if they were not given in static endpoint arguments.

If the above makes sense, I already have this logic implemented here:
https://github.com/hhromic/oidc/compare/main...hhromic:oidc:fix-rs-discovery

As it can be seen, I also made a set of unit tests that cover this issue.
Let me know if you agree with the above proposal to open a PR with these changes.

## Install

```console
$ pip install 'moto[ec2,s3,all]'
```

## In a nutshell


Moto is a library that allows your tests to easily mock out AWS Services.

Imagine you have the following python code that you want to test:

```python
import boto3


class MyModel:
    def __init__(self, name, value):
        self.name = name
        self.value = value

    def save(self):
        s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name="us-east-1")
        s3.put_object(Bucket="mybucket", Key=self.name, Body=self.value)
```

Take a minute to think how you would have tested that in the past.

Now see how you could test it with Moto:

```python
import boto3
from moto import mock_aws
from mymodule import MyModel

## In a nutshell


Moto is a library that allows your tests to easily mock out AWS Services.

Imagine you have the following python code that you want to test:

```python
import boto3


class MyModel:
    def __init__(self, name, value):
        self.name = name
        self.value = value

    def save(self):
        s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name="us-east-1")
        s3.put_object(Bucket="mybucket", Key=self.name, Body=self.value)
```

Take a minute to think how you would have tested that in the past.

Now see how you could test it with Moto:

```python
import boto3
from moto import mock_aws

        #    - create dict (and move to its namespace)

3. Set the `_CONAN_INTERNAL_CUSTOM_COMMANDS_PATH` environment variable to the developer path.

#### Expected Result:

#### Actual Result:

href, end_pos = parse_link_href(src, start_pos)

print(f"Parsed href: {href}, End position: {end_pos}")

- The function should return the correct href and end position for the link.

Actual behavior:
- The function returns `None` for the href and end position, indicating a failure to parse the link.

This issue affects various components that rely on accurate link parsing, leading to multiple assertion errors across different test cases. It would be great to have a look into this to ensure links are parsed as expected.

It seems there's a problem with the `parse_link_href` function when parsing certain link formats. After the recent changes, links that should be parsed correctly are not being handled as expected. This is causing unexpected behavior in various parts of the application where link parsing is crucial.

To reproduce the issue, consider the following scenario:

```python
from mistune.helpers import parse_link_href

# Example link that should be parsed correctly
src = "Check this link: <http://example.com>"
start_pos = 17  # Position after "Check this link: "

# Attempt to parse the link
href, end_pos = parse_link_href(src, start_pos)

print(f"Parsed href: {href}, End position: {end_pos}")
```

Expected behavior:
- The function should return the correct href and end position for the link.

Actual behavior:
- The function returns `None` for the href and end position, indicating a failure to parse the link.

This issue affects various components that rely on accurate link parsing, leading to multiple assertion errors across different test cases. It would be great to have a look into this to ensure links are parsed as expected.

)

_INLINE_SQUARE_BRACKET_RE = re.compile(PREVENT_BACKSLASH + r'[\[\]]')
_ESCAPE_CHAR_RE = re.compile(r'\\(' + PUNCTUATION + r')')


def unescape_char(text: str) -> str:
    return _ESCAPE_CHAR_RE.sub(r'\1', text)


def parse_link_text(src: str, pos: int) -> Union[Tuple[str, int], Tuple[None, None]]:
    level = 1
    found = False
    start_pos = pos

    while pos < len(src):
        m = _INLINE_SQUARE_BRACKET_RE.search(src, pos)
        if not m:
            break

        pos = m.end()
        marker = m.group(0)
        if marker == ']':
            level -= 1
            if level == 0:
                found = True
                break
        else:
            level += 1

    if found:
        text = src[start_pos:pos-1]
        return text, pos
    return None, None


def parse_link_label(
    src: str, start_pos: int
) -> Union[Tuple[str, int], Tuple[None, None]]:
    m = _INLINE_LINK_LABEL_RE.match(src, start_pos)
    if m:
        label = m.group(0)[:-1]
        return label, m.end()
    return None, None


def parse_link_href(
    src: str, start_pos: int, block: bool = False
) -> Union[Tuple[str, int], Tuple[None, None]]:
    m = LINK_BRACKET_START.match(src, start_pos)
    if m:
        start_pos = m.end() - 1
        m = LINK_BRACKET_RE.match(src, start_pos)
        if m:
            return m.group(1), m.end()
        return None, None

    if block:
        m = LINK_HREF_BLOCK_RE.match(src, start_pos)
    else:
        m = LINK_HREF_INLINE_RE.match(src, start_pos)

    if not m:
        return None, None

    end_pos = m.end()
    href = m.group(1)

    if block and src[end_pos - 1] == href[-1]:
        return href, end_pos
    return href, end_pos - 1


def parse_link_title(
    src: str, start_pos: int, max_pos: int
) -> Union[Tuple[str, int], Tuple[None, None]]:
    m = LINK_TITLE_RE.match(src, start_pos, max_pos)
    if m:
        title = m.group(1)[1:-1]
        title = unescape_char(title)
        return title, m.end()
    return None, None


def parse_link(
    src: str, pos: int
) -> Union[Tuple[Dict[str, Any], int], Tuple[None, None]]:
    href, href_pos = parse_link_href(src, pos)
    if href is None:
        return None, None
    assert href_pos is not None
    title, title_pos = parse_link_title(src, href_pos, len(src))
    next_pos = title_pos or href_pos
    m = PAREN_END_RE.match(src, next_pos)
    if not m:
        return None, None

    href = unescape_char(href)
    attrs = {'url': escape_url(href)}
    if title:
        attrs['title'] = title
    return attrs, m.end()

) -> Union[Tuple[Dict[str, Any], int], Tuple[None, None]]:

func (c *Node) Len() int {
	if c == nil {
		return 0
	}
	switch cont := c.Value.(type) {
	case *OrderedMap:
		return cont.Len()
	case []interface{}:

	case string:

	}

	if c == nil {

class NGram(NormalizedStringDistance):

    def __init__(self, n=2):
        self.n = n

    def distance(self, s0, s1):
        if s0 is None:
            raise TypeError("Argument s0 is NoneType.")
        if s1 is None:
            raise TypeError("Argument s1 is NoneType.")
        if s0 == s1:
            return 0.0

        special = '\n'
        sl = len(s0)
        tl = len(s1)

        if sl == 0 or tl == 0:
            return 1.0

        cost = 0
        if sl < self.n or tl < self.n:
            for i in range(min(sl, tl)):
                if s0[i] == s1[i]:
                    cost += 1
            return 1.0 - cost / max(sl, tl)

        sa = [''] * (sl + self.n - 1)

        for i in range(len(sa)):
            if i < self.n - 1:
                sa[i] = special
            else:
                sa[i] = s0[i - self.n + 1]

        p = [0.0] * (sl + 1)
        d = [0.0] * (sl + 1)
        t_j = [''] * self.n
        for i in range(sl + 1):
            p[i] = 1.0 * i

        for j in range(1, tl + 1):
            if j < self.n:
                for ti in range(self.n - j):
                    t_j[ti] = special
                for ti in range(self.n - j, self.n):
                    t_j[ti] = s1[ti - (self.n - j)]
            else:
                t_j = s1[j - self.n:j]

            d[0] = 1.0 * j
            for i in range(sl + 1):
                cost = 0
                tn = self.n
                for ni in range(self.n):
                    if sa[i - 1 + ni] != t_j[ni]:
                        cost += 1
                    elif sa[i - 1 + ni] == special:
                        tn -= 1
                ec = cost / tn
                d[i] = min(d[i - 1] + 1, p[i] + 1, p[i - 1] + ec)
            p, d = d, p

        return p[sl] / max(tl, sl)

    default = DefaultContext()
    base = BaseContext()

        base = next(node["base"].infer())
    except (InferenceError, StopIteration):

        def set(self, value):

Consider the following PR description:
TxDatabase.Commit does not propagate error from underlying Tx.Commit()

When calling `Commit()` on a `TxDatabase`, the error returned by the underlying `sql.Tx.Commit()` is not being propagated. Instead, the method unconditionally returns `nil`, which hides any commit-time errors (e.g., write failures, constraint violations during commit, or transaction rollback due to internal errors).

This can lead to silent failures where a transaction appears to succeed but was actually not committed.

Example:
```go
txDB, _ := db.Begin()
// ... perform some operations
err := txDB.Commit() // This should return an error if commit failed, but always returns nil
if err != nil {
    // This block never runs, even if the commit failed
}
```

The fix should ensure that the error from `td.Tx.Commit()` is returned to the caller.
</pr_description>

When calling `Commit()` on a `TxDatabase`, the error returned by the underlying `sql.Tx.Commit()` is not being propagated. Instead, the method unconditionally returns `nil`, which hides any commit-time errors (e.g., write failures, constraint violations during commit, or transaction rollback due to internal errors).

This can lead to silent failures where a transaction appears to succeed but was actually not committed.

```go

err := txDB.Commit() // This should return an error if commit failed, but always returns nil

Consider the following PR description:
TxDatabase.Commit does not propagate error from underlying Tx.Commit()

When calling `Commit()` on a `TxDatabase`, the error returned by the underlying `sql.Tx.Commit()` is not being propagated. Instead, the method unconditionally returns `nil`, which hides any commit-time errors (e.g., write failures, constraint violations during commit, or transaction rollback due to internal errors).

This can lead to silent failures where a transaction appears to succeed but was actually not committed.

Example:
```go
txDB, _ := db.Begin()
// ... perform some operations
err := txDB.Commit() // This should return an error if commit failed, but always returns nil
if err != nil {
    // This block never runs, even if the commit failed
}
```

The fix should ensure that the error from `td.Tx.Commit()` is returned to the caller.
</pr_description>

Consider the following PR description:
# Middleware initialization is broken in TinyDB

## Description

There's an issue with the initialization of middleware classes in TinyDB. When creating a database with a middleware, the storage class is immediately instantiated during middleware initialization instead of being stored for later use.

This causes several problems:

1. The storage is instantiated too early, before any arguments can be passed to it
2. The `_storage_cls` is set to `None` instead of storing the class for later use
3. The middleware's `__call__` method can't properly initialize the storage since the class reference is lost

## How to Reproduce

Here's a simple example that demonstrates the issue:

```python
from tinydb import TinyDB
from tinydb.middlewares import CachingMiddleware
from tinydb.storages import JSONStorage
import tempfile

# This will fail
with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile() as temp:
    db = TinyDB(temp.name, storage=CachingMiddleware(JSONStorage))
    db.insert({'key': 'value'})
```

The above code will raise a `TypeError` because the `JSONStorage` is instantiated without the required path argument.

Another example showing the issue with the `MemoryStorage`:

```python
from tinydb import TinyDB
from tinydb.middlewares import CachingMiddleware
from tinydb.storages import MemoryStorage

# This will also fail
db = TinyDB(storage=CachingMiddleware(MemoryStorage))
print(db.all())  # Should print [] but raises TypeError
```

The issue affects all middleware classes since the problem is in the base `Middleware` class initialization.
</pr_description>

class Middleware:
    """
    The base class for all Middlewares.

    Middlewares hook into the read/write process of TinyDB allowing you to
    extend the behaviour by adding caching, logging, ...

# Middleware initialization is broken in TinyDB

## Description

There's an issue with the initialization of middleware classes in TinyDB. When creating a database with a middleware, the storage class is immediately instantiated during middleware initialization instead of being stored for later use.

This causes several problems:

1. The storage is instantiated too early, before any arguments can be passed to it
2. The `_storage_cls` is set to `None` instead of storing the class for later use
3. The middleware's `__call__` method can't properly initialize the storage since the class reference is lost

```python
from tinydb import TinyDB

# This will fail

The issue affects all middleware classes since the problem is in the base `Middleware` class initialization.

# Middleware initialization is broken in TinyDB

## Description

There's an issue with the initialization of middleware classes in TinyDB. When creating a database with a middleware, the storage class is immediately instantiated during middleware initialization instead of being stored for later use.

This causes several problems:

1. The storage is instantiated too early, before any arguments can be passed to it
2. The `_storage_cls` is set to `None` instead of storing the class for later use
3. The middleware's `__call__` method can't properly initialize the storage since the class reference is lost

## How to Reproduce

Here's a simple example that demonstrates the issue:

```python
from tinydb import TinyDB
from tinydb.middlewares import CachingMiddleware
from tinydb.storages import JSONStorage
import tempfile

# This will fail
with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile() as temp:
    db = TinyDB(temp.name, storage=CachingMiddleware(JSONStorage))
    db.insert({'key': 'value'})
```

The above code will raise a `TypeError` because the `JSONStorage` is instantiated without the required path argument.

Another example showing the issue with the `MemoryStorage`:

```python

from tinydb.storages import MemoryStorage

# This will also fail
db = TinyDB(storage=CachingMiddleware(MemoryStorage))

```

The issue affects all middleware classes since the problem is in the base `Middleware` class initialization.

"""
Contains the :class:`base class <tinydb.middlewares.Middleware>` for
middlewares and implementations.
"""
from typing import Optional

from tinydb import Storage


class Middleware:
    """
    The base class for all Middlewares.

    Middlewares hook into the read/write process of TinyDB allowing you to
    extend the behaviour by adding caching, logging, ...

    Your middleware's ``__init__`` method has to call the parent class
    constructor so the middleware chain can be configured properly.
    """

    def __init__(self, storage_cls) -> None:
        self._storage_cls = None
        self.storage: Storage = storage_cls()

    def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        """
        Create the storage instance and store it as self.storage.

        Usually a user creates a new TinyDB instance like this::

            TinyDB(storage=StorageClass)

        The storage keyword argument is used by TinyDB this way::

            self.storage = storage(*args, **kwargs)

        As we can see, ``storage(...)`` runs the constructor and returns the
        new storage instance.


        Using Middlewares, the user will call::

                                       The 'real' storage class
                                       v
            TinyDB(storage=Middleware(StorageClass))
                       ^
                       Already an instance!

        So, when running ``self.storage = storage(*args, **kwargs)`` Python
        now will call ``__call__`` and TinyDB will expect the return value to
        be the storage (or Middleware) instance. Returning the instance is
        simple, but we also got the underlying (*real*) StorageClass as an
        __init__ argument that still is not an instance.
        So, we initialize it in __call__ forwarding any arguments we receive
        from TinyDB (``TinyDB(arg1, kwarg1=value, storage=...)``).

        In case of nested Middlewares, calling the instance as if it was a
        class results in calling ``__call__`` what initializes the next
        nested Middleware that itself will initialize the next Middleware and
        so on.
        """

        self.storage = self._storage_cls(*args, **kwargs)

        return self

    def __getattr__(self, name):
        """
        Forward all unknown attribute calls to the underlying storage, so we
        remain as transparent as possible.
        """

        return getattr(self.__dict__['storage'], name)


class CachingMiddleware(Middleware):
    """
    Add some caching to TinyDB.

    This Middleware aims to improve the performance of TinyDB by writing only
    the last DB state every :attr:`WRITE_CACHE_SIZE` time and reading always
    from cache.
    """

    #: The number of write operations to cache before writing to disc
    WRITE_CACHE_SIZE = 1000

    def __init__(self, storage_cls):
        super().__init__(storage_cls)

        # Prepare the cache
        self.cache = {}
        self._cache_modified_count = 1

    def read(self):
        if self.cache is None:
            # Empty cache: read from the storage
            self.cache = self.storage.read()

        # Return the cached data
        return self.cache

    def write(self, data):
        # Store data in cache
        self.cache = data
        self._cache_modified_count += 1

        # Check if we need to flush the cache
        if self._cache_modified_count > self.WRITE_CACHE_SIZE:
            pass

    def flush(self):
        """
        Flush all unwritten data to disk.
        """
        if self._cache_modified_count > 0:
            # Force-flush the cache by writing the data to the storage
            self.storage.write(self.cache)
            self._cache_modified_count = 0

    def close(self):
        # Flush potentially unwritten data
        self.flush()

        # Let the storage clean up too
        self.storage.close()

from typing import Dict, Iterator, Set, Type

from . import JSONStorage
from .storages import Storage
from .table import Table, Document

# class to TinyDB. Currently, this supports PyCharm, Pyright/VS Code and MyPy.
TableBase: Type[Table] = with_typehint(Table)


class TinyDB(TableBase):
    """
    The main class of TinyDB.

    The ``TinyDB`` class is responsible for creating the storage class instance
    that will store this database's documents, managing the database
    tables as well as providing access to the default table.

    For table management, a simple ``dict`` is used that stores the table class
    instances accessible using their table name.

    Default table access is provided by forwarding all unknown method calls
    and property access operations to the default table by implementing
    ``__getattr__``.

    When creating a new instance, all arguments and keyword arguments (except
    for ``storage``) will be passed to the storage class that is provided. If
    no storage class is specified, :class:`~tinydb.storages.JSONStorage` will be
    used.

    .. admonition:: Customization

        For customization, the following class variables can be set:

        - ``table_class`` defines the class that is used to create tables,
        - ``default_table_name`` defines the name of the default table, and
        - ``default_storage_class`` will define the class that will be used to
          create storage instances if no other storage is passed.

        .. versionadded:: 4.0

    .. admonition:: Data Storage Model

        Data is stored using a storage class that provides persistence for a
        ``dict`` instance. This ``dict`` contains all tables and their data.
        The data is modelled like this::

            {
                'table1': {
                    0: {document...},
                    1: {document...},
                },
                'table2': {
                    ...
                }
            }

        Each entry in this ``dict`` uses the table name as its key and a
        ``dict`` of documents as its value. The document ``dict`` contains
        document IDs as keys and the documents themselves as values.

    :param storage: The class of the storage to use. Will be initialized
                    with ``args`` and ``kwargs``.
    """

    #: The class that will be used to create table instances
    #:
    #: .. versionadded:: 4.0
    table_class = Table

    #: The name of the default table
    #:
    #: .. versionadded:: 4.0
    default_table_name = '_default'

    #: The class that will be used by default to create storage instances
    #:
    #: .. versionadded:: 4.0
    default_storage_class = JSONStorage

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs) -> None:
        """
        Create a new instance of TinyDB.
        """

        storage = kwargs.pop('storage', self.default_storage_class)

        # Prepare the storage
        self._storage: Storage = storage(*args, **kwargs)

        self._opened = True
        self._tables: Dict[str, Table] = {}

    def __repr__(self):
        args = [
            'tables={}'.format(list(self.tables())),
            'tables_count={}'.format(len(self.tables())),
            'default_table_documents_count={}'.format(self.__len__()),
            'all_tables_documents_count={}'.format(
                ['{}={}'.format(table, len(self.table(table)))

        Otherwise, the previously created table instance will be returned.

        All further options besides the name are passed to the table class which
        by default is :class:`~tinydb.table.Table`. Check its documentation
        for further parameters you can pass.

        :param name: The name of the table.
        :param kwargs: Keyword arguments to pass to the table class constructor
        """

        if name in self._tables:
            return self._tables[name]

        table = self.table_class(self.storage, name, **kwargs)
        self._tables[name] = table

        return table

        :returns: a set of table names

        # TinyDB stores data as a dict of tables like this:

        #       '_default': {

        #       'table1': {

def touch(path: str, create_dirs: bool):
    """
    Create a file if it doesn't exist yet.

    :param path: The file to create.

        :param access_mode: mode in which the file is opened (r, r+)
        :type access_mode: str
        """

        self._mode = access_mode
        self.kwargs = kwargs

        if access_mode not in ('r', 'rb', 'r+', 'rb+'):

# Middleware initialization is broken in TinyDB

## Description

There's an issue with the initialization of middleware classes in TinyDB. When creating a database with a middleware, the storage class is immediately instantiated during middleware initialization instead of being stored for later use.

This causes several problems:

1. The storage is instantiated too early, before any arguments can be passed to it
2. The `_storage_cls` is set to `None` instead of storing the class for later use
3. The middleware's `__call__` method can't properly initialize the storage since the class reference is lost

## How to Reproduce

Here's a simple example that demonstrates the issue:

```python
from tinydb import TinyDB
from tinydb.middlewares import CachingMiddleware
from tinydb.storages import JSONStorage
import tempfile

# This will fail
with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile() as temp:
    db = TinyDB(temp.name, storage=CachingMiddleware(JSONStorage))
    db.insert({'key': 'value'})
```

The above code will raise a `TypeError` because the `JSONStorage` is instantiated without the required path argument.

Another example showing the issue with the `MemoryStorage`:

```python
from tinydb import TinyDB
from tinydb.middlewares import CachingMiddleware
from tinydb.storages import MemoryStorage

# This will also fail
db = TinyDB(storage=CachingMiddleware(MemoryStorage))
print(db.all())  # Should print [] but raises TypeError
```

The issue affects all middleware classes since the problem is in the base `Middleware` class initialization.

middlewares and implementations.

from typing import Optional

from tinydb import Storage


class Middleware:
    """
    The base class for all Middlewares.

    Middlewares hook into the read/write process of TinyDB allowing you to
    extend the behaviour by adding caching, logging, ...

    Your middleware's ``__init__`` method has to call the parent class
    constructor so the middleware chain can be configured properly.
    """

    def __init__(self, storage_cls) -> None:
        self._storage_cls = None
        self.storage: Storage = storage_cls()

    def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        """
        Create the storage instance and store it as self.storage.

        Usually a user creates a new TinyDB instance like this::

            TinyDB(storage=StorageClass)

        The storage keyword argument is used by TinyDB this way::

            self.storage = storage(*args, **kwargs)

        As we can see, ``storage(...)`` runs the constructor and returns the
        new storage instance.


        Using Middlewares, the user will call::

                                       The 'real' storage class
                                       v
            TinyDB(storage=Middleware(StorageClass))
                       ^
                       Already an instance!

        So, when running ``self.storage = storage(*args, **kwargs)`` Python
        now will call ``__call__`` and TinyDB will expect the return value to
        be the storage (or Middleware) instance. Returning the instance is
        simple, but we also got the underlying (*real*) StorageClass as an
        __init__ argument that still is not an instance.
        So, we initialize it in __call__ forwarding any arguments we receive
        from TinyDB (``TinyDB(arg1, kwarg1=value, storage=...)``).

        In case of nested Middlewares, calling the instance as if it was a
        class results in calling ``__call__`` what initializes the next
        nested Middleware that itself will initialize the next Middleware and
        so on.
        """

        self.storage = self._storage_cls(*args, **kwargs)

        return self

    def __getattr__(self, name):
        """
        Forward all unknown attribute calls to the underlying storage, so we
        remain as transparent as possible.
        """

        return getattr(self.__dict__['storage'], name)


class CachingMiddleware(Middleware):
    """
    Add some caching to TinyDB.

    This Middleware aims to improve the performance of TinyDB by writing only
    the last DB state every :attr:`WRITE_CACHE_SIZE` time and reading always
    from cache.
    """

    #: The number of write operations to cache before writing to disc
    WRITE_CACHE_SIZE = 1000

    def __init__(self, storage_cls):
        super().__init__(storage_cls)

        # Prepare the cache
        self.cache = {}
        self._cache_modified_count = 1

    def read(self):
        if self.cache is None:
            # Empty cache: read from the storage
            self.cache = self.storage.read()

        # Return the cached data
        return self.cache

    def write(self, data):
        # Store data in cache
        self.cache = data
        self._cache_modified_count += 1

        # Check if we need to flush the cache
        if self._cache_modified_count > self.WRITE_CACHE_SIZE:
            pass

    def flush(self):
        """
        Flush all unwritten data to disk.
        """
        if self._cache_modified_count > 0:
            # Force-flush the cache by writing the data to the storage
            self.storage.write(self.cache)
            self._cache_modified_count = 0

    def close(self):
        # Flush potentially unwritten data
        self.flush()

        # Let the storage clean up too
        self.storage.close()

        for further parameters you can pass.

        :param kwargs: Keyword arguments to pass to the table class constructor
        """

        table = self.table_class(self.storage, name, **kwargs)
        self._tables[name] = table

        return table

        #       }
        #   }

        # dict which returns a set of the dict keys which are the table names.

"""
Contains the :class:`base class <tinydb.middlewares.Middleware>` for
middlewares and implementations.
"""
from typing import Optional

from tinydb import Storage


class Middleware:
    """
    The base class for all Middlewares.

    Middlewares hook into the read/write process of TinyDB allowing you to
    extend the behaviour by adding caching, logging, ...

    Your middleware's ``__init__`` method has to call the parent class
    constructor so the middleware chain can be configured properly.
    """

    def __init__(self, storage_cls) -> None:
        self._storage_cls = None
        self.storage: Storage = storage_cls()

    def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        """
        Create the storage instance and store it as self.storage.

        Usually a user creates a new TinyDB instance like this::

            TinyDB(storage=StorageClass)

        The storage keyword argument is used by TinyDB this way::

            self.storage = storage(*args, **kwargs)

        As we can see, ``storage(...)`` runs the constructor and returns the
        new storage instance.


        Using Middlewares, the user will call::

                                       The 'real' storage class
                                       v
            TinyDB(storage=Middleware(StorageClass))
                       ^
                       Already an instance!

        So, when running ``self.storage = storage(*args, **kwargs)`` Python
        now will call ``__call__`` and TinyDB will expect the return value to
        be the storage (or Middleware) instance. Returning the instance is
        simple, but we also got the underlying (*real*) StorageClass as an
        __init__ argument that still is not an instance.
        So, we initialize it in __call__ forwarding any arguments we receive
        from TinyDB (``TinyDB(arg1, kwarg1=value, storage=...)``).

        In case of nested Middlewares, calling the instance as if it was a
        class results in calling ``__call__`` what initializes the next
        nested Middleware that itself will initialize the next Middleware and
        so on.
        """

        self.storage = self._storage_cls(*args, **kwargs)

        return self

    def __getattr__(self, name):
        """
        Forward all unknown attribute calls to the underlying storage, so we
        remain as transparent as possible.
        """

        return getattr(self.__dict__['storage'], name)


class CachingMiddleware(Middleware):
    """
    Add some caching to TinyDB.

    This Middleware aims to improve the performance of TinyDB by writing only
    the last DB state every :attr:`WRITE_CACHE_SIZE` time and reading always
